Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit.

We represent: appellant defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a sentencing court commits procedural error when it fails to adequately explain an upward variance.

Cite at least six decisions of the Eighth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. The District Court Committed Procedural Error by Failing to Adequately Explain the Upward Variance.**

**A. Standard of Review and Governing Law**

This Court reviews the reasonableness of a sentence under a deferential abuse-of-discretion standard. *Gall v. United States*, 552 U.S. 38, 51 (2007); *United States v. Feemster*, 572 F.3d 455, 461 (8th Cir. 2009) (en banc). The review has two steps. The Court first asks whether the district court committed "significant procedural error." That category includes failing to consider the 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a) factors and "failing to adequately explain the chosen sentence—including an explanation for any deviation from the Guidelines range." *Gall*, 552 U.S. at 51; *Feemster*, 572 F.3d at 461. Only if the sentence is procedurally sound does the Court turn to substantive reasonableness. *Feemster*, 572 F.3d at 461.

The explanation requirement is not a formality. A sentencing judge must "set forth enough to satisfy the appellate court that he has considered the parties' arguments and has a reasoned basis for exercising his own legal decisionmaking authority." *Rita v. United States*, 551 U.S. 338, 356 (2007). When the judge imposes a sentence outside the Guidelines range, the explanation must carry more weight. Under *Gall*, a court that decides an outside-Guidelines sentence is warranted "must consider the extent of the deviation and ensure that the justification is sufficiently compelling to support the degree of the variance." 552 U.S. at 50. This Court, sitting en banc, applies the same rule. *Feemster*, 572 F.3d at 461–62. The Court has also repeatedly held that a bare recital of the § 3553(a) factors, or a conclusory statement that a variance is "appropriate," does not satisfy this duty. *See United States v. Lozoya*, 623 F.3d 624, 626 (8th Cir. 2010); *United States v. Miner*, 544 F.3d 930, 932 (8th Cir. 2008); *United States v. Roberson*, 517 F.3d 990, 994 (8th Cir. 2008).

**B. The Explanation Here Does Not Meet That Standard**

The district court varied upward from the advisory Guidelines range of [__] months and imposed a sentence of [__] months. That is [__] months, or [__] percent, above the top of the range. A variance of that size required a correspondingly compelling justification. *Gall*, 552 U.S. at 50; *Feemster*, 572 F.3d at 461–62.

The court did not provide one. It [describe: recited the § 3553(a) factors in general terms / pointed only to the seriousness of the offense / did not identify any fact that the Guidelines range had failed to take into account]. The Guidelines already account for the seriousness of the offense and for [Appellant's] criminal history. A sentencing court that varies upward on those grounds must say why this case is different from the heartland the Commission contemplated. *See Roberson*, 517 F.3d at 994; *United States v. Wiley*, 509 F.3d 474, 476 (8th Cir. 2007). The record does not show that the court did so. Nor does it show that the court weighed the mitigating arguments defense counsel raised, including [identify arguments], or explain why it rejected them. *Rita* requires that showing. 551 U.S. at 356.

This Court has remanded where a district court's explanation left it unable to tell why the court chose a sentence outside the range. *See Lozoya*, 623 F.3d at 626; *Miner*, 544 F.3d at 932; *United States v. Whitlow*, 815 F.3d 430, 435 (8th Cir. 2016). Those decisions control. Appellate review is meaningful only when the district court's reasoning appears in the record. The Court should not have to supply a rationale the sentencing judge never gave. *See Feemster*, 572 F.3d at 461–62.

**C. The Error Was Preserved and Requires Resentencing**

[Defense counsel objected to the variance and to the adequacy of the court's explanation at sentencing. J.A. __.] If the objection was not preserved, the error still satisfies plain-error review. The omission was clear under *Gall* and *Feemster*. It affected [Appellant's] substantial rights, because nothing in the record shows that the court would have imposed the same above-Guidelines sentence had it considered the required factors and explained its reasons. It also undermines the fairness and integrity of the proceedings, because a defendant cannot know why he received [__] months above the range.

Because the procedural error is significant, the Court need not reach substantive reasonableness. It should vacate the sentence and remand for resentencing with an adequate explanation. *Feemster*, 572 F.3d at 461.
